paper_title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

Introduction Hospitals are 3D environments where small spatial errors carry clinical consequences [19, 37]. nurse walking through ward knows which bed lit bed-head light belongs to, what lies on the patients left, and whether transport bed can pass bedside cart. MLLMs supporting hospital assistants need to make these judgments from egocentric video. This is challenging because similar equipment repeats across beds, the patients left and right may differ from the viewers, and passage depends on both obstacle geometry and equipment width. Existing benchmarks evaluate spatial reasoning in general scenes [4, 21, 23, 35, 47, 49], but provide limited coverage of patient-relative directions, equipment ownership, and width-constrained passage. This requires videos with clear visual evidence and accurate spatial annotations. Collecting such data in hospitals is difficult because of patient privacy and the cost of measuring scene geometry. We therefore use simulation to construct hospital scenes with controlled layouts and scene-derived answers. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench  (Fig. 1)  , with 3,368 questions across eight question types and 373 layouts spanning 16 hospital room types  (Fig. 2)  . Layouts follow constraints derived from hospital design guidelines, and answers are computed from the underlying 3D scenes, including routes and passage widths. Paired states of the same layout differ in one scene condition, such as which bedhead light is on, allowing us to test whether models change their answers when the relevant evidence changes. Rendered walkthroughs are converted to photorealistic videos and checked for camera-path consistency. Ten physicians screened the layouts, reviewing one video per layout. We also provide Clinical3D-45K, training set with 44,750 questions from layouts disjoint from the benchmark. We evaluate 32 open MLLMs and three proprietary models, and fine-tune two models on Clinical3D-45K. The best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy. For reference, test-fitted answer prior scores 40.8%, and physicians score 79.0% on 400-question subset. Patient-relative directions are particularly challenging: 27 of the 32 open zero-shot models score below 40%, against 50% chance. Fine-tuning VideoJev-4B [57] raises its macro accuracy from 45.5% to 73.9% and its patientframe accuracy from 17.0% to 93.7%. On paired states with different correct answers, evaluated zero-shot models retain the same answer more often than their answer preferences predict; fine-tuning reduces this excess repetition. However, route planning and passability remain the fine-tuned models weakest tasks, at 58.3% and 66.0%, respectively. These results motivate testing whether explicit 3D input [11, 33, 42] can improve spatial reasoning. However, adding birds-eye-view (BEV) tokens [32], local map reads, or geometry head during MLLM fine-tuning yields no clear gain in overall accuracy. For BEV tokens and local map reads, replacing the correct map with another clips barely changes accuracy; the ground-truth map setting shows the same pattern. These findings motivate computing evidence from 3D representations and using it directly to score answer options. To this end, we introduce GeoJeV (Sec. 5, Fig. 5), which reconstructs scene memory from each video and uses three 3D primitives for object-track queries, free-space analysis, and learned BEV map reads. Linear heads on the fine-tuned VideoJev-4Bs question state select primitive and its arguments, and the resulting evidence is added to the models option scores. This requires no second language model. GeoJeV improves macro accuracy from 73.9% to 75.7%, with gains mainly in counting, re-identification, passability, and direction; route accuracy improves only from 58.3% to 59.5%. Replacing its scene memory with another layouts lowers accuracy to 70.4%, showing that its predictions depend on scene-specific evidence. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Clinical3DBench, hospital spatial reasoning benchmark with scenederived answers and paired scene states, accompanied by Clinical3D-45K. (2) An evaluation of 35 MLLMs and finetuning experiments that reveal persistent difficulties in route planning and passability, alongside limited gains from the tested 3D input strategies. (3) GeoJeV, framework that selects 3D computations from an MLLMs question state and combines their evidence with option scores, improving accuracy over the fine-tuned baseline. 2. Related work Spatial benchmarks for MLLMs. Existing benchmarks test spatial reasoning from videos [47], multiple images [49], online observations [23], and different viewpoints [21]. VSI-Bench includes human-annotated routes. SAT and SIMS-V generate spatial questions through simulation [4, 35], while Open3D-VQA uses real and simulated aerial scenes [52]. Clinical3D-Bench evaluates patientrelative directions, equipment relations, and routes and passage widths computed from hospital scene occupancy. Paired scene states with different correct answers test whether models respond to changes in the scene (Tab. 1). Clinical spatial reasoning. Medical VQA benchmarks focus on medical images [15, 16, 20], including 3D spatial reasoning in SpatialMed [38]. MM-OR and EgoExOR study surgical scenes and activities [58, 59], while ORExpert addresses operating-room spatial reasoning [14]. Clinical3D-Bench complements these tasks with patientrelative directions, equipment ownership, and clearanceconstrained navigation across diverse hospital rooms. 2 Table 1. Clinical3D-Bench 3.1. Overview We introduce Clinical3D-Bench to measure the 3D spatial intelligence of MLLMs in hospital rooms from egocentric video. It has 3,368 multiple-choice questions on 569 tensecond clips of 373 layouts in 16 room families. Scenes are generated in simulation from hospital design standards and every answer is computed from the scene record; the clips are transferred to photorealistic appearance, verified against the scene and screened by physicians. disjoint training set, Clinical3D-45K, has 44,750 questions. 3 Figure 3. Construction of Clinical3D-Bench. Top: construction with paired-state example (abridged). Blue marks clearance-check regions; bedside/foot zones allow movable equipment. Bottom: checks and retained counts. Regenerating passage-width questions leaves nine screened layouts without questions, giving the final 373 layouts and 569 clips. Tasks. The eight question types form four task groups (Fig. 2; shares in Fig. 4a). Spatial memory: Count asks how many instances of category seen so far are out of view at given time, and Re-ID asks which instance at later time is the one named earlier. Ownership and relations: Light owner asks which bed the lit bed-head light belongs to, and Device reference asks what device is mounted on or which label it carries, where the device is named by its relation to bed or landmark and look-alike is in view. Frames of reference: Patient frame asks whether an object is on the left or right of patient on named bed; no people are present, so the model imagines supine patient, and left and right are the patients. Metric navigation: Direction asks for the first change of direction on the shortest walkable route from the cameras start pose to goal, or for the goals quadrant; Route asks to fill in the turn sequence of that route or for the goal nearest by walking; Passability asks whether passage wide enough for crash cart (0.9 m) or transport bed (1.2 m) reaches the goal. The types comprise 15 subtasks (Tab. 6). Construction. Clinical3D-Bench is built in five steps  (Fig. 3)  : scenes are generated from hospital design standards (Sec. 3.2), questions are generated and checked (Sec. 3.3), clips are transferred to photorealistic appearance (Sec. 3.4), and physicians screen the layouts (Sec. 3.5). 3.2. Standards-grounded scene generation From standards to rules. Hospital planning standards state how large room must be and how much free space its beds need. We take these requirements for each room type from three public standards (UK Health Building Notes, Australasian Health Facility Guidelines, US VA Space Planning Criteria), recording the source section of each, and use them in three ways. Size requirements, such as room area and the spacing between beds, set the ranges from which layouts dimensions are sampled. Clearance requirements become geometric checks: clear strip of 0.9 beside each ward bed (1.5 in ICU), clear zone at the foot of the bed and free zone at the door. Functional requirements become checks on content and access: every bed position has service panel and the required pumps, the room has handwash station, drawn curtains do not block the entry, and every bed foot can be reached from the door. Each of the 16 room families has generator program [9, 34, 50], and layout is kept only if it passes every check  (Fig. 3)  ; random seeds are fixed, so every layout can be regenerated. Assets, rendering and clips. Free-standing equipment (beds, IV poles, patient monitors, ventilators, imaging and surgical units, chairs, carts; 22 of 47 object categories) uses NVIDIA SimReady assets [29] (CC BY 4.0). Everything else is built procedurally: the parts that questions depend on (infusion pumps with bed labels, bed-head panels, surgical lights and ceiling pendants, curtains, doors, bed labels), equipment with no suitable SimReady model (CT, stretcher, sharps containers, sanitiser dispensers) and other furniture (Sec. A); small wall items are placed by clinical rules. camera then walks through the room at eye height (1.55 m, 90 horizontal field of view) along path that passes every bed and comes close enough to each label to read it; it moves at 0.40.9 m/s and turns at most 30/s. The walk is path-traced in Blender at 768448 and 6 fps, and every frame is stored with metric depth, instance and part masks, and the camera intrinsics and pose. From each walk we keep one 10 clip (60 frames), the window in which the most candidate questions can be answered; all questions are asked on this clip. Paired states. layout is built in up to three states that differ in one clinical fact: the lit bed-head light (in corridors, the lit nurse-call light) moves to another bed or room, the privacy curtains change, or corridor items move. All states of layout share one clip window, and each state is one clip. In the final set 111 of the 373 layouts keep two or three states. Questions instantiated from the same template on the states of one layout form paired group of two or three questions; the final set has 262 groups, and in 204 of them the correct answer changes. 3.3. Question generation and quality control Questions are instantiated from templates over the scene record. Three groups of checks, all computed from the rendered ground truth, make them answerable and unambiguous (thresholds in the supplement). Evidence: every object, part or label question depends on must be visible, above pixel threshold and for at least 1 s, in the 32 frames model receives. Margins: referring expressions must pick out one object by clear distance margin, and near-boundary questions are removed, such as near-ties in walking distance and passability answers that do not hold 0.1 either side of the stated width. Shortcuts: answer values are balanced within each subtask, and blind filter [5] of two text-only models and text-statistics test flags 739 of 3,368 questions (21.9%); they stay in the official score, and the debiased score excludes them. Model-in-the-loop refinement: subtask formulations that zero-shot or blind models answered near ceiling were replaced by harder ones. Refinement acted on formulations, not on individual questions, but since it used Qwen3-VL-8B and -32B, their scores on Clinical3D-Bench may be biased downward relative to other models. 3.4. Photorealistic clips Renders are geometrically exact but look synthetic, while generative video transfer [28] looks real but carries no 3D ground truth. We use generators for appearance only and verify their output against the scene. Keyframes are edited with an image model (gpt-image-2 [30]), and the render plus edited keyframes condition video-to-video model (MiniMax-H3 [27]). Each clip is registered to its render by feature matching [10, 24] and PnP on the rendered depth, and passes if 75% of its frames lie on the source path; 649 of 657 clips pass, with median pose error 0.03 and 0.5 (supplement). The gate verifies the camera path, not that every evidence object survives the transfer: the questions inherit the render-side evidence checks, and the physician screen removes layouts with visible artefacts. All results use the photorealistic clips; training clips are renders. 3.5. Clinical screening and final set Screening. Ten resident physicians took part. They first reviewed each question type, and we revised the wording where they asked, checking that no answer changed. They then rated one photorealistic clip of every layout that passed the pose gate (437 clips, two physicians each) on three 0 5 scales: layout plausibility, realism and clinical usability (means 4.25 / 4.31 / 4.36; Fig. 4b). Is 3D given as input used? Shuffle twins. For 3D-augmented model we evaluate twin whose 3D comes from another clip at test time; the model uses the scenes 3D only if its twin is clearly worse. We test four ways of giving fine-tuned MLLM 3D (Tab. 3): Lift-Splat [32] BEV tokens appended to the visual tokens, local BEV reads injected into the language model, geometry head on its hidden states, and, as privileged input, ground-truth BEV maps. With BEV tokens, local reads or the ground-truth map, the twin is within 0.5 points of the real model. The geometry head does read the scene (1.4 points lower with another clips 3D) but adds only 0.6 points over the plain fine-tune. No 3D input thus lifts the model clearly above it, and GeoJeV instead adds 3D as computation outside the MLLM. 5.2. GeoJeV Fine-tuning helps; planning lags. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K lifts VideoJev-4B from 45.5 to 73.9 (three seeds), yet Route (58.3) and Passability (66.0) remain its weakest types, while Patient frame rises from 17.0 to 93.7. GeoJeV builds on VideoJev4B [57], which encodes the question and each option and scores option with cosine decision head on its final hidden states, ℓ(o) = cos(Wqhq, Woho) + b, and pM(o V, q) = softmaxo ℓ(o) for frames and question q. Because each option has its own score, 3D evidence about an option can be added to that option directly. The model is fine-tuned on Clinical3D-45K and then frozen. Scene memory. Each clip is reconstructed once from its RGB frames: VGGT [40] gives depth and camera poses, detector [17] gives objects, which are lifted to 3D and linked into tracks, and Lift-Splat encoder [32] gives semantic birds-eye-view (BEV) map and 3D object boxes. The memory holds the tracks with their time stamps, the boxes, the walkable floor and the BEV map; no benchmark depth, pose, mask or label is used. Three primitives. memory looks up the tracks of one class: how many are out of view at time t, how many there are in all, or which detection at is the same object as the leftor rightmost one at t. free_space searches the walkable floor around the object boxes for the widest body that still gets from start to goal. geometry, which serves the remaining spatial questions, has no arguments: learned map reader takes the question and option text, makes few hard reads of cells of the BEV map and scores It is trained by on-policy distileach option from them. lation [1, 13, 36] from privileged teacher [8] that reads ground-truth maps. memory and free_space take arguments (an object class, times, start and goal, width), never the questions wording. The MLLM calls the primitives. Let hq be the MLLMs question state, the decision heads query input. Linear heads on hq give the primitive, π = route(hq), and its arguments θ = args(hq): object classes, the side of the reference, and which number of the question is time or width. No head predicts the question type or the operation. The router needs no question-type labels: its target is the set of primitives that alone answer training question correctly, so question goes where 3D computation helps. No second language model is involved, and the heads add no forward pass (details of all parts in the supplement). 5.3. Results of GeoJeV GeoJeV improves the fine-tuned MLLM. Over three fine-tuning seeds, GeoJeV raises the macro from 73.9 to 75.7, each seed with its own heads (+1.8, paired layoutbootstrap 95% CI [+0.7, +3.0]; every seeds gain is above zero). The gains sit on the types the primitives target (Tab. 2): Count and Re-ID (memory, +2.5 and +3.9), Passability (free_space, +3.8) and Direction (geometry, +3.4); the other types change by 1.2 points or less. Each primitive contributes, and the scenes 3D is used. Removing any one primitive costs 0.30.7 points, each on its own types (Tab. 4). Given another layouts scene memory (same room family, same state), GeoJeV falls to 70.4, 3.5 points below the MLLM alone, with Re-ID at 55.7 instead of 77.8 and Count at 62.1 instead of 69.3: unlike the 3D inputs of Sec. 5.1, the evidence it adds is specific to the scene. Conclusion Clinical3D-Bench measures 3D spatial intelligence in hospital rooms with exact, scene-derived answers, answerchanging scene states and pose-verified photorealistic clips. Zero-shot MLLMs stay close to the answer prior and fail at the patients frame of reference; fine-tuning supplies that convention but leaves route planning and passability the weakest types. 3D added to the fine-tuned model as input is left largely unused, whereas GeoJeV lets an option-scoring MLLM call 3D primitives from its own hidden state and add their evidence to its per-option scores.

Scene assets Of the 47 object categories in the benchmark scenes, 22 use NVIDIA SimReady assets [29] and 25 are built procedurally (Tab. 5). We place each SimReady model in the same local frame as the procedural meshes it replaces. We keep the procedural parts that questions refer to (e.g. bed and chair number plates) on top of the model. B. Question definitions and quality-control thresholds Types and subtasks. subtask is single question form for which we balance answer values separately. We group the 15 subtasks into the eight question types used in the main paper (Tab. 6). Accuracy per type pools the questions of its subtasks. Navigation. Routes are shortest paths on 0.1 occupancy grid with 0.35 body clearance. Walking distance is measured to the nearest standable cell beside the goal. Direction changes under 30 are ignored and changes over 135 count as turning around. The starting point is the cameras pose in the first frame or the foot of labelled bed. Route plans can also start next to named object, with the walker facing another. Goals are clinical cues: the bed whose bed-head light is on, unique device such as crash cart, handwash station or patient monitor, bed by its plate, or the room whose nurse-call light is on. Distractors. Light owner offers cannot be determined as distractor. In Mount and Label, look-alike device of the same class is in view, so the model must identify the target device by its relation to the named bed or landmark. Evidence. We keep question only if each evidence item appears in one of the 32 frames model receives and is visible for at least 1 without interruption in the clip (Device reference: the first condition only). The minimum visible areas are 400 pixels for an object, 60 for part such as lamp or label, and 90 for text that must be read. Re-ID uses its two named frames instead: the target is the leftmost instance at t, and shows two or three instances, each of 1,500 pixels, clear of the image border and 40 pixels apart. If the target is not among them (77 of 195 questions), the answer is not in that frame. Count question is dropped if any instance is only partly visible (at least 30 pixels but never reaching the counting threshold). Margins. Referring expressions must pick out one object. In Mount, the runner-up device must be at least 0.3 farther from the landmark than the nearest device and at least 1/0.85 times as far. In Label, it must be at least 0.5 farther. The following near-boundary questions are removed: quadrant questions within 20 of quadrant boundary; nearest-by-walking questions won by under 0.6 m; routes whose turn sequence changes when the body clearance grows by 0.1 m, or that have legs under 0.8 or turns of 3045; passage-width questions whose widest passable width is not 0.10.35 from the stated width, and straight routes cleared or blocked by under 0.15 m. When selecting questions, we cap the share of each answer value at min(0.55, 1/k+0.1) within its subtask or within finer group where cue could reveal the answer (e.g. within each wording template). Here counts the values at least tenth as frequent as the most common one. In Count, 4 or more falls below that threshold, so = 4 and the cap is 35%. We cap each answer value in Quadrant at 27%. For passage-width questions, we cap yes at 55% for each stated width. Route distractors follow the trainingsplit frequency of turn sequences, and each clip contributes capped number of questions per subtask. Blind filter. The blind filter gives the question and options to two text-only models, Qwen3-VL-8B and -32B [2]. It also uses naive-Bayes text-statistics test cross-validated by layout. The filter flags question if both models answer it correctly or the test assigns the gold answer probability of 0.8. For the passage-width questions only the textstatistics test applies. For each camera path, we select the 10 window (60 frames) with the most answerable candidates, summed over the states walked along the path and weighted by 1/ subtask candidate count; candidate counts if its evidence is visible for 1 inside the window.
